title: South African Seed certification legislation, rules and procedures

lessons.title: The legal and institutional framework
lessons.html:
Why seed is certified

A farmer cannot tell by looking at a bag of seed whether it is the cultivar named on the label, whether it is genetically pure, or whether it will germinate. Seed certification is an independent system that verifies varietal identity and purity through controlled multiplication, field inspection, sampling and testing. It protects farmers, breeders and the reputation of South African seed in export markets.

Legislation

  • Plant Improvement Act 53 of 1976 and its regulations: the main law on the sale of seed and plant material, variety listing, registration of businesses and premises dealing with seed, and minimum quality standards. A new Plant Improvement Act was passed in 2018; check with your organisation which provisions and regulations are currently in force.
  • Plant Breeders' Rights legislation: protects the intellectual property of breeders in new varieties.
  • Agricultural Pests Act 36 of 1983: relevant for phytosanitary control of plant material and seed imports.

Institutions

  • Department of Agriculture: the national authority responsible for the Plant Improvement Act, variety listing and the national seed certification scheme.
  • SANSOR (South African National Seed Organisation): the industry body to which certain certification functions are delegated; it administers the scheme day to day for many crops.
  • Accredited seed testing laboratories that perform official tests.
  • International schemes: the OECD Seed Schemes for seed in international trade, and ISTA for testing rules and certificates.

Variety listing

Only varieties on the national variety list may be certified and sold for most controlled crops. Listing requires that a variety is distinct, uniform and stable (DUS), and for some crops that it has value for cultivation and use.

Seed classes (generations)

Certified seed is produced in limited generations from the breeder's original material to stop genetic drift and contamination:

  1. Breeder seed (maintained by the breeder)
  2. Pre-basic seed
  3. Basic seed
  4. Certified seed (first and, for some crops, second generation)

Each class has its own label colour and standards under the scheme.

lessons.title: Certification procedures from field to label
lessons.html:
Step by step

1. Registration and application

Seed growers, processors and sellers must be registered as required. The grower applies to enter a field (seed crop) into the scheme, providing the variety, seed class sown, proof of the parent seed (labels and lot numbers), field location and area, and previous cropping history.

2. Field requirements

  • Previous cropping: the field must not have grown the same or a related crop recently enough for volunteer plants to contaminate the seed crop.
  • Isolation: minimum distances from other crops that could cross-pollinate, which are much greater for cross-pollinated crops such as maize and sunflower than for self-pollinated crops such as wheat or soybeans.
  • Parent seed: must be of the correct, higher class.

Specific distances and periods are set in the scheme rules for each crop; always use the current rules.

3. Field inspection

Authorised inspectors examine the crop at the growth stages specified, often around flowering. They count off-types, other varieties, other crop species, noxious weeds and seed-borne diseases against the standards, check isolation and assess whether roguing was effective. A field that fails may be rejected or downgraded.

4. Harvest, processing and identity

Harvested seed must keep its identity. Combines, trucks and processing plants must be cleaned between lots to prevent mixing. Processing units clean, grade, treat and pack seed into lots with lot numbers.

5. Sampling and testing

Authorised samplers sample each lot according to ISTA rules. Laboratories test purity, germination, other seeds and, where required, moisture and varietal purity. Results must meet the minimum standards for the class.

6. Labelling and sealing

Lots that pass receive official certification labels and seals for their class. Labels carry information such as crop, variety, class, lot number and test results as required.

7. Post-control

Samples of certified lots may be grown in control plots to verify varietal identity and purity, which checks the whole system.

Key points

  • Certification verifies varietal identity and purity through controlled generations.
  • The Plant Improvement Act 53 of 1976 and scheme rules govern certification; confirm current provisions.
  • Only listed varieties meeting DUS criteria can be certified.
  • Fields must meet cropping history, isolation and parent seed requirements.
  • Lots are sampled, tested, labelled and post-controlled.
